title: Redis data structures
summary: The core Redis structures — strings, lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets, streams, bitmaps, HyperLogLog and geospatial — with the key commands and time complexity the exam tests.

blocks.body:
Redis is usually introduced as a key-value store, but that framing undersells it.
Every value in Redis is a **typed data structure** — the key is only the name you
use to reach it. `TYPE` tells you what a key holds, and the type decides which
commands work on it: you cannot `LPUSH` onto a hash, and `HGET` against a set is
a wrong-type error, not a coercion.

That one idea drives a large share of the certification exam: know what each
structure is for, the commands that operate on it, and what each operation costs.

## Strings: the default workhorse

A string value holds text, a serialized blob, or a number — up to 512 MB per value.

```redis
SET session:user-42 "active" EX 3600
INCR metrics:pageviews            # atomic counter, O(1)
APPEND audit:log " entry"         # O(1) amortized
MGET config:a config:b            # one round trip, two keys
```

Key commands: `GET`, `SET` (with `EX`/`PX` expiry and `NX`/`XX` modifiers),
`SETNX`, the atomic counter family `INCR` / `DECR` / `INCRBY` / `INCRBYFLOAT`,
`APPEND`, `STRLEN`, `GETRANGE` / `SETRANGE`, and `MGET` / `MSET`.

`GET` and `SET` are O(1), and so is the counter family. Because `INCR` is atomic,
counters and the `SET ... NX` lock idiom need no application-side locking — a
point the exam returns to often.

## Lists: ordered sequences at the ends

Lists are ordered collections of strings, optimized for pushes and pops at both
ends — the classic queue and stack structure.

```redis
LPUSH queue:emails "job-1"        # O(1)
RPOP queue:emails                 # O(1) — LPUSH + RPOP is a FIFO queue
LRANGE queue:emails 0 9           # O(S+N) — slice of the list
LINDEX queue:emails 500           # O(N) — walks from the nearest end
LTRIM queue:emails 0 999          # keep only the newest 1000
```

`LMOVE` (blocking form `BLMOVE`) atomically moves an element between two lists
and is the building block of reliable worker queues; `BLPOP` / `BRPOP` let idle
consumers block instead of polling.

Random access into the middle is O(N), so lists fit queues, stacks, and
recent-activity feeds — not lookup tables. Small lists are stored as a compact
`listpack`; larger ones become a `quicklist` of listpack segments.

## Hashes: one object per key

A hash maps fields to string values — the natural fit for one object (user,
product, session) per key.

```redis
HSET user:42 name "Ada" role "admin" logins 7
HINCRBY user:42 logins 1          # O(1), atomic per field
HGET user:42 name                 # O(1)
HGETALL user:42                   # O(N) in the number of fields
```

Per-field commands are O(1): `HSET`, `HGET`, `HMGET`, `HEXISTS`, `HDEL`,
`HINCRBY`, `HSETNX`. Whole-hash reads — `HGETALL`, `HKEYS`, `HVALS` — are O(N)
in the field count, which matters when objects are wide. Small hashes use the
compact `listpack` encoding (tuned by `hash-max-listpack-entries`), one of the
most memory-efficient ways to store an object in Redis.

## Sets: unordered, unique membership

Sets hold unique strings with no order and constant-time membership tests.

```redis
SADD followers:42 "u7" "u9"       # O(1) per member
SISMEMBER followers:42 "u7"       # O(1)
SINTER followers:42 followers:43  # who both users follow
SDIFF followers:42 followers:43   # in 42 but not in 43
SINTERSTORE common:42-43 followers:42 followers:43
```

`SCARD` is O(1); `SMEMBERS` is O(N); set algebra — `SINTER`, `SUNION`, `SDIFF` —
is worst-case O(N·M) across the sets involved, and `SINTERCARD` caps the work
with a `LIMIT`. A set of small integers under `set-max-intset-entries` is stored
as a compressed `intset`. Typical uses: tags, unique visitors, relationships,
deduplication.

## Sorted sets: order maintained for you

Sorted sets are sets in which every member carries a score, and members are kept
ordered by score — Redis's answer to leaderboards, priority queues, time-window
indexes, and range queries.

```redis
ZADD leaderboard 9820 "ada" 9750 "grace"
ZINCRBY leaderboard 30 "grace"             # O(log N) — re-ranks in place
ZRANGE leaderboard 0 2 REV WITHSCORES      # top three, O(log N + M)
ZRANK leaderboard "grace"                  # O(log N) — zero-based position
ZRANGEBYSCORE events:2026-09-03 0 +inf     # score-range scan
```

The split the exam tests: `ZSCORE` and `ZCARD` are O(1); ranked operations —
`ZADD`, `ZINCRBY`, `ZRANK`, `ZRANGE`, `ZRANGEBYSCORE`, `ZREM` — are O(log N),
plus M for members actually returned. Two idioms to recognize: bumping a score
with `ZINCRBY` to re-rank, and using a timestamp as the score to build a
time-ordered index you can slice by range.

## Streams: append-only logs with consumer groups

A stream is an append-only log of entries. Every entry has an ID of the form
`<milliseconds>-<sequence>` and one or more field-value pairs. Entries are
immutable — you append with `XADD` and delete with `XDEL`, but you never edit
in place.

```redis
XADD orders * user 42 item "sku-9" total 19.99    # * auto-generates the ID
XRANGE orders - + COUNT 10                        # read a range
XLEN orders                                       # O(1)
XADD orders MAXLEN ~ 1000000 * user 7 item "sku-2"
```

`XADD` is O(1). Trimming supports `MAXLEN` (keep roughly the newest N) and
`MINID` (drop everything older than an ID), and `~` lets Redis trim in blocks
instead of exact counts — far cheaper on large streams.

**Consumer groups** let many clients share one stream without each tracking its
own position:

- `XGROUP CREATE orders order-workers $` — `$` starts the group at new entries
  only; `0` replays the stream's whole history.
- `XREADGROUP GROUP order-workers worker-1 COUNT 10 BLOCK 5000 STREAMS orders >`
  — `>` delivers entries never delivered to this group.
- Reading with ID `0` instead of `>` re-delivers the consumer's own pending
  entries — the recovery path after a crash.
- Each group tracks a **last-delivered ID**; each consumer gets a **PEL**
  (pending-entries list) of delivered-but-unacknowledged IDs.
- `XACK` marks an entry fully processed. `XPENDING` inspects the PEL;
  `XCLAIM` / `XAUTOCLAIM` take over entries stranded by a dead consumer.

This is the at-least-once delivery machinery the exam likes to probe: delivery,
acknowledgement, and crash recovery are explicit steps — unlike pub/sub, where
an unread message is simply gone.

## Bitmaps: booleans at one bit each

A bitmap is an ordinary string value that you address bit by bit — 100 million
one-bit flags fit in roughly 12 MB.

```redis
SETBIT active:2026-09-03 42819 1        # O(1) — user 42819 active today
GETBIT active:2026-09-03 42819          # O(1)
BITCOUNT active:2026-09-03              # O(N) — how many users were active
BITOP AND active:week active:2026-09-02 active:2026-09-03   # O(N)
BITPOS active:2026-09-03 1              # first set bit
```

`SETBIT` and `GETBIT` are O(1); `BITCOUNT`, `BITOP`, and `BITPOS` are O(N) in
the bytes scanned. The daily-mask pattern — one bitmap per day, `BITOP AND` or
`OR` across days for retention analysis — is the canonical use case.

## HyperLogLog: counted, never listed

A HyperLogLog estimates cardinality — how many *unique* elements were added —
using a fixed ~12 KB per key with a standard error of about 0.81%.

```redis
PFADD visits:2026-09-03 "u1" "u2" "u1"    # duplicates cost nothing
PFCOUNT visits:2026-09-03                 # ~2, effectively O(1)
PFMERGE visits:week visits:2026-09-02 visits:2026-09-03   # O(N)
```

`PFADD` is O(1) and single-key `PFCOUNT` is effectively O(1); multi-key
`PFCOUNT` and `PFMERGE` are O(N). The trade-off is total: you get the count but
never the members back — at large scale that beats a set by orders of magnitude.

## Geospatial: locations as a sorted set

The geo commands store longitude/latitude pairs in a **sorted set** under the
hood — each member is a place name and its score is a 52-bit geohash encoding
of the coordinates.

```redis
GEOADD cities 13.3614 48.8566 "paris" 2.3522 48.8566 "chartres"
GEOSEARCH cities FROMLONLAT 2.3522 48.8566 BYRADIUS 100 km ASC COUNT 5
GEODIST cities paris chartres km
GEOPOS cities paris
```

`GEOADD` is O(log N) per location; `GEOSEARCH` answers radius and nearest-first
queries. Because the container is a sorted set, re-adding an existing name
overwrites its coordinates rather than erroring — a favorite exam trap.

## Cost at a glance

| Structure | Write | Point read | Range / whole |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| String | O(1) SET | O(1) GET | O(N) GETRANGE |
| List | O(1) LPUSH/RPUSH | O(N) LINDEX | O(S+N) LRANGE |
| Hash | O(1) per field | O(1) HGET | O(N) HGETALL |
| Set | O(1) SADD | O(1) SISMEMBER | O(N) SMEMBERS |
| Sorted set | O(log N) ZADD | O(1) ZSCORE | O(log N + M) ZRANGE |
| Stream | O(1) XADD | O(N) | O(N) XRANGE |
| Bitmap | O(1) SETBIT | O(1) GETBIT | O(N) BITCOUNT/BITOP |
| HyperLogLog | O(1) PFADD | O(1) PFCOUNT | O(N) PFMERGE |
| Geo | O(log N) GEOADD | O(1) GEOPOS | O(N+log M) GEOSEARCH |

## Exam takeaways

- `TYPE` reveals the structure; wrong-type commands are errors, never coercions.
- Lists: ends O(1), middle O(N). Hashes and sets: per-element O(1),
  whole-structure O(N).
- Sorted sets trade O(log N) writes for maintained order; `ZSCORE` stays O(1).
- Streams: entries are immutable, IDs are `<ms>-<seq>`, each group keeps a
  last-delivered ID and per-consumer PELs, and `XACK` completes delivery.
- Bitmaps are strings addressed by bit; HyperLogLog is a fixed-size estimate
  with no member recall; geospatial is a sorted set in disguise.
